articles.body: The South African-born jurist and former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay, who is currently an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law. Her win is sure to be seen as a high-profile rebuke to US President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of a UN commission she led that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Both leaders also have been highly critical of the institutions where Pillay has worked. FRANCE 24's International Affairs Editor Philip Turle tells us more.
articles.headline: Navi Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in international justice

articles.body: A big win for Zimbabwean literature: Harare-based author Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza has claimed the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing for his short story "The Blue Fighter". The award is given to the best short story by an African writer published in English and comes with a £10,000 pounds cash prize. FRANCE 24's Sharon Mazingaizo met with the writer.
articles.headline: 'The Blue Fighter': Zimbabwean author Kundizeza wins 2026 Caine Prize

articles.body: The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Thursday opened its hearing into Senegal's appeal against being stripped of the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title in favour of Morocco. The hearing in Lausanne comes almost 10 months after Pape Gueye's extra-time goal gave Senegal victory over the tournament hosts following a chaotic finish to normal time. But in March, the Confederation of African Football (CAF) overturned that result, awarding Morocco a 3-0 victory, and the title.
articles.headline: Senegal, Morocco to get AFCON title verdict within days

articles.body: A Kenyan national who had been living in Congo before returning to Nairobi has become Kenya’s first confirmed Ebola case and the country’s first fatality from the disease in the rapidly evolving outbreak. The Kenya Red Cross is supporting the government’s efforts to prevent a public health crisis. FRANCE 24’s Bastien Renouil met with Paul Olala, the NGO’s head of health security and emergencies.
articles.headline: Kenya Red Cross supports response to country’s first Ebola case

articles.body: The fight against Ebola poses a challenge in the Central African Republic. In Zemio, in the country’s south-east, proximity to the Democratic Republic of Congo has raised fears that the virus could spread across the border. But health screening remains difficult. The repeated absence of health workers at checkpoints is hampering surveillance, while residents continue to cross the border through unofficial crossing points, as FRANCE 24's team on the ground reports.
articles.headline: Ebola outbreak: Border surveillance gaps raise concerns in the Central African Republic

articles.body: The first US military execution in more than 65 years will be livestreamed, announced the Pentagon on Thursday, after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said it would be "public". Former Army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan opened fire at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, killing 13 people. His execution will take place at the military base on December 3, 2026. "The livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture," the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said on Friday.
articles.headline: Pentagon vows to livestream first military execution in decades

articles.body: Ten months after the explosive AFCON final, Senegal and Morocco are still fighting over the title, this time at sport's highest court. A verdict on Senegal's appeal against Morocco's victory by default is expected within days. Also, it's a race against time in Kenya. Health officials are tracing dozens of contacts after an Ebola patient died following a journey from DR Congo. Plus Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza wins the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing for his short story "The Blue Fighter".
articles.headline: Court of Arbitration for Sport hears Senegal's appeal over AFCON title

articles.body: The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution on December 3 of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree, a Pentagon official said, in what would be an unprecedented move. Hasan, a former ​Army psychiatrist, is ‌set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945.
articles.headline: US to livestream Army execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon official says

articles.body: Erin Ogunkeye welcomes Dr. Antoine Marie, postdoctoral researcher, fellow and lecturer at Sciences Po / CEVIPOF, to explore the political psychology behind France’s student protests. Why do people witness the same events yet reach radically different conclusions about violence? Dr Marie examines how media echo chambers, partisan thinking and the politicization of empathy deepen polarization, making it easier to overlook the suffering of those perceived as political opponents. He also examines France’s increasingly offensive police doctrine, questions surrounding accountability, and the institutional incentives that may actually hinder independent investigations into police misconduct.

articles.body: One in four Trump voters say GOP candidates should break with the president to win in November, according to the latest POLITICO Poll , conducted by independent firm PF Global. The findings underscore the degree to which even loyal Republicans understand President Donald Trump is a drag on the ticket. Persistent inflation, $4 gas prices, 7% mortgage rates, a quagmire in the Middle East and a trade war with Canada have given Republican candidates no shortage of opportunities to take the president to task. Michigan’s GOP Senate candidate Mike Rogers this week became the latest example when he called for an end to the “tariff war” with Canada — a notable shift after he spent weeks defending the president’s decision. “It was brilliant by Mike Rogers … when you talk about the affordability issue, in every poll I get back, every week, more and more people have this as their top issue,” said Michigan-based GOP consultant Jason Roe, who is working on Rep. Tom Barrett’s (R-Mich.) reelection campaign. “Obviously the price of gas is a result of the Iran war, and in Michigan, more than anything else, the trade war with Canada.” Rogers is hardly the only example. Florida GOP Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar used an ad filmed in front of the White House to call out the president’s immigration crackdown. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), in her bid to win the Iowa Senate seat, has called for an end to the Iran war amid souring diesel costs. Ken Paxton, the GOP’s embattled Texas Senate nominee, has now been the subject of four leaks exposing his private attempts to distance himself from Trump and the national party. “It’s just all dictated by the data,” said a GOP strategist working on a Senate campaign, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the president. “They see the writing on the wall about the gas prices and the inflation. Running as a Trump sycophant is not going to work in 2026. It’s the only political move you can do in Michigan, a state like that. It’s toxic to be tied to the man.” There are some limits: No Republican has completely broken with Trump, and several are eager to stand next to him on stage or in the Oval. Few dare to criticize him directly. And many still lean on their ties to the president on the campaign trail and in their social media profiles as they seek to rally the MAGA base. A White House official, granted anonymity to discuss internal thinking, scoffed at the idea that Rogers’ — or any other candidates’ — efforts to distance themselves from Trump administration policies, amounted to a major break with the president. “If I’m a candidate that’s physically trying to push away from the president, I’m not attending this stuff. I’m just gonna back away all the way,” the official said. “Being in the midst of a campaign and needing to talk to the issues that are being discussed as kitchen table topics, you just kind of have to.” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle pointed to the Trump administration’s efforts to lower prescription drug costs, cut taxes, secure the border and grow job numbers: “No one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the president understands how to communicate with them. President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.” Politicians touting their independence from Washington is nothing new. But as the poll reveals, it’s notable that so many who voted for Trump, who has been the GOP's dominant force for a decade, are ready for candidates to take that leap. Much of the fracture is driven by the non-MAGA wing of his coalition, the people who voted for Trump in 2024 but do not identify as part of his most loyal base, the survey found. When asked about specific issues such as the economy, trade and tariffs, data centers, immigration and the Iran war, non-MAGA Trump voters were roughly twice as likely as MAGA Trump voters to say their GOP candidate should break from the president. But Trump still retains an intense hold over the base. More than two-thirds of MAGA voters said GOP candidates should continue to align with Trump across all of those issues. That creates a no-win situation for many Republican candidates: Tie yourself to Trump and his policies too tightly and you lose independents and non-MAGA Republicans. Break too far, and you risk leaving MAGA disenchanted. Candidates trying to thread that needle are quick to praise the president but blame his advisers, as Salazar did, or avoid mentioning Trump by name at all. Roe said each candidate has to measure the “downstream effects” of a decision to distance themselves from the president, adding that it’s a balance between “alienating your base with appealing to voters that are looking for some independence.” On the campaign trail, many Republicans acknowledge that the president remains an asset in shoring up base voters crucial to November. It’s part of the reason Trump has aggressively traveled to red states — including Alabama, Alaska, Iowa, Nebraska, Ohio and Texas — bastions of conservatism that need his star power to coax die-hard supporters to the polls. The White House official pointed to the president’s rally with South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham ahead of her run-off as an example of Trump’s ability to juice turnout. RNC press secretary Natalie Baldassarre insisted that Republicans “remain united behind the president’s agenda” and are “laser focused on winning.” “Our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control,” she said. The president is telling voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot, and he has insisted the party is already in a better place as he blitzes states across the country, touting his economy and arguing that higher prices are a small price to pay for national security amid the lingering war with Iran. But some candidates are still nervous that if they campaign beside the president, they could alienate undecided voters. Some Republicans have encouraged Trump’s team not to send the president to a blue-leaning Omaha district and other key districts where his approval rating is underwater ahead of Election Day. “I don’t think there are that many candidates who are clamoring for Trump to come to their state. But to the extent they do, it’s a gamble that they’ve already lost the voters who are gonna vote against them, and they need to light a fire under the voters who are sitting it out, and he’s the torch,” said Democratic strategist David Axelrod, who was chief strategist for Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign. “The problem is the torch can burn the whole house down.” The damned-if-you-do, damned-if-you-don’t dilemma is perhaps best captured with Paxton’s campaign in Texas. On Wednesday, Trump took the stage in San Antonio, bringing up Paxton, the same day his latest closed-door comments complaining about the Iran war and high prices dragging down his campaign went public. But standing on stage with Trump, he struck a much different tune. “Wow, what is it like to be up on stage with the president of the United States? Pretty amazing,” he said. “Mr. President, I want to thank you for coming for me, for coming for us and for coming for Texas.”
articles.headline: Even Trump voters think Republicans should split from the president to win

articles.body: In late September, top Republicans across House GOP leadership, leading political operations and individual campaigns received a trove of internal polling. It sparked a new level of panic. The polling didn’t just reveal a harsh environment for the party in power on par with typical midterms, but rather some close-to-catastrophic scenarios in a slew of formerly safe red seats across the country, according to three people with direct knowledge of the matter who were granted anonymity to discuss private information. Key seats in Kentucky, North Carolina, Nevada and other areas that President Donald Trump won by 10 points or more in 2024 were competitive. All three vulnerable GOP-held seats in Iowa looked doomed. And most ominously, a crop of Republican incumbents who haven’t had to run serious races in years were vulnerable, from Oklahoma to Wisconsin and beyond. Now, less than four weeks before Election Day, the concerns are running so deep and the atmosphere is so uncertain that Republicans are beginning to brace for some of the worst-case scenarios. "Polls aren't looking good,” retiring Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.) said in an interview. “But we've also seen in the past couple of cycles, polls are really hard to predict. I think there's just a lot of things in play, and of course, what do we have three weeks out — that's light years in political time.” One senior House Republican involved in the conversations added: “I think the scary part is we don’t know where the bottom is.” They, like others in this report, were granted anonymity to discuss the political climate honestly. Their worst fear — according to conversations with more than two dozen Republican lawmakers and senior operatives — is that white working class voters in some states who have become central to the GOP coalition won’t just stay home next month, but instead they’ll be so angry or disillusioned by high fuel prices and the war in Iran that enough of them will vote for Democrats. “The environment has a lot people scared to death,” said one GOP operative working on a red-leaning House race that is competitive. “Where is the surge in Dem votes coming from?” that operative asked. “Is it truly no turnout among white working class? It's such an open question and we just don't know the answer. It's impossible.” Spokespeople for the National Republican Congressional Committee and the Republican National Committee brushed off the concerns. "Anonymous strategists who spend more time bed-wetting to media than working in the trenches to win races have no idea what they're talking about,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said. NRCC spokesperson Mike Marinella agreed: “House Republicans have a more favorable map, a stronger ground game, a historic fundraising and spending advantages, and battle-tested incumbents while Democrats are stuck dragging their unelectable socialist nominees across the finish line.” Still, top Republicans’ travel schedule reveals the extent of their concerns: Johnson is heading to deep-red Kentucky on Friday for a fundraiser to boost Republican Ralph Alvarado in the 6th District, which Trump won by 15 points in 2024. Johnson and Trump are also both planning trips to Montana where Republicans are working to fend off a Democratic challenger in a district the president won by more than 11 points. “Speaker Johnson is leaving it all on the field and leaving no stone unturned as he campaigns in more than 40 districts and over 20 states in the month leading up to the election,” Johnson’s spokesperson Greg Steele said. And, pointing to Johnson’s record-setting third quarter funding, Steele added that: “Johnson is not slowing down and helping to get resources to every district that will decide the majority.” Trump is holding a rally in deep-red Tennessee on Saturday, in GOP Rep. Matt Van Epps’ district. That seat — which is still considered generally safe — and several others in the state have not been on Republicans’ radar at all, but the current drag of the war and other factors are just too big for them to be comfortable. “I’m worried about all three in the area,” one Tennessee Republican said of the red-leaning districts Democrats are targeting. “Too many unknowns.” Even as internal GOP data shows a series of troubles, Republicans argue the polls are overemphasizing Democrats’ advantage. “I think there’s no question there is some undersampling,” said one RNC official, granted anonymity to discuss internal deliberations. “I’m not surprised any of these are close. I’m not surprised that Democrats are trying to make it seem like we’re on defense everywhere,” they said. “These are never [races] that we assumed were overall slam dunks, but I very much like where we sit in all of them.” Still, the person added that RNC officials don’t have their “heads in the sand” about the challenges, even as they have a more optimistic view of the map. Loudermilk pointed to Republicans’ lack of cohesive messaging on high gas prices and other goods: “I don’t know if we’re doing a good enough job doing that.” “It’s not the best of environments,” Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.) told reporters in late September, though he still maintained the GOP will keep House control. “I liked it a lot better when I first got elected in 2010, when the environment was much better for Republicans.” Top Republicans are most worried about staunching the bleeding in key Midwest districts. Senior Republicans believe their internal polling, if it holds, shows likely losses across all three at-risk GOP seats in Iowa: Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks and the race to replace now-Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, according to four people with direct knowledge of the private information. A White House official, granted anonymity to candidly discuss the races, said the “doom and gloom notion” among the Iowa seats isn’t a new phenomenon. “But I do think that they’re probably performing better than most think that they are. And I think that folks will be pleasantly surprised [when] we go into November 3.” But benchmarks they’re watching across the larger region are deteriorating as well. Wisconsin Rep. Bryan Steil, the House Administration chair, is in a tighter than comfortable race after winning by 11 points in 2024 — as is Rep. Brad Finstad across the border in Minnesota, who won his district by 12 points 2024. In Michigan, the party has a host of problems in battleground districts, but now feels that once-safer seat Republicans — like Bill Huizenga, who Johnson campaigned with Wednesday, and the race to replace Rep. John James, who is running for governor — are in jeopardy. Similarly, after top GOP outside groups cut bait on the blue-leaning Nebraska district held by retiring Rep. Don Bacon, Republicans in the state turned their attention to Rep. Mike Flood’s seat, which Trump carried by 12 points. One silver lining for Republicans in safer red seats is many are digging in now to shore up their races, and aren’t sleepwalking to November. The White House official said it’s Trump’s “coalition of voters” that Republicans need to turn out in the midterms, and “the president is on the road almost every night this month … communicating with those individuals.” But Democrats continue to stretch further into red territory while forecasting big wins. “We feel confident that we will get to 218,” Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee political director Brooke Butler said in an interview earlier this week , saying the party could win as many as 240 seats. “The question that I’ve told people from the beginning cycle is ‘How much?’” But while Democrats are increasingly bullish, they are navigating their own tough decisions because of Republicans’ massive cash advantage , leaving the GOP optimistic they can hold a few seats where Democrats don’t have the resources to compete. Top GOP House operatives remain confident about a number of core battleground districts — including where candidates have already put some distance between themselves and Trump. One national party operative remained hopeful that as Election Day nears, the races will get closer than polling currently suggests, as has been the case in past cycles. That would help them hold some of these redder seats that are competitive. Even as Republicans hope some red seats fall off the board as Election Day nears, many operatives told POLITICO they’re worried that outside groups will have to start siphoning resources into red areas to shore them up, moving important dollars out of the battlegrounds. “People that are in R+10 districts are showing [polling that] they’re tied and they're saying, ‘I need help,’” said a GOP operative working on a battleground House race. “There's real opportunity for Democrats in a lot of these.” Rep. French Hill, the chair of the Financial Services Committee from deep-red Arkansas whose opponent was just added to the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” list, said in a recent interview with POLITICO that he considers “the atmosphere a very tough political environment right now because of President [Donald] Trump’s lack of favorability at the top, and you know people are concerned about, as I say, what it’s like to live under an inflated economy the last four years.” Johnson, an eternal optimist, made clear during a campaign stop in Pennsylvania this week that he believes “this will be a close election.” He’s ramping up his warnings across the campaign trail of what Democrats winning power would mean: “They would try to impeach the president, of course, immediately …They’d spend every waking hour investigating the president, his family, and the cabinet, and leaders of business and industry. That would roil the markets. Just ask yourself, if you're a hardworking family, how would that be for your family? That Democrats turned Congress into lawfare on steroids.” Samuel Benson contributed to this report.
articles.headline: House Republicans are bracing for catastrophe in once safe red seats

articles.body: The progressive political action committee Justice Democrats has appointed Rev. Hodari Williams as its new executive director. The change sets the organization up to hone a civil rights message ahead of the 2028 election cycle, Williams told POLITICO. His appointment, shared first with POLITICO, comes at a time when self-proclaimed progressives (and socialists) are flooding the scene. The PAC has had its most successful election cycle ever, helping seven candidates — including Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Melat Kiros in Colorado and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York — defeat incumbents in the primaries. While those candidates are heavily favored to win on Election Day, the fates of three other Justice Democrats candidates, including Tennessee’s state Rep. Justin Pearson, remain less certain going into November. At one point, the group tried to get Williams to run for office. Though he declined, Williams said now is the right time to force change. “America and its present-day politicians, from my experience, have a high blood pressure of promises and anemia of political courage,” Williams said in an interview, using a common Kenyan political expression. “Right now, JD is producing candidates who have the political courage to deal with the crises that are existing in marginalized and disenfranchised communities, and I want to be a part of that.” Williams, 46, was born and raised in Lakewood, New Jersey. His parents were activists and community organizers who raised him on the legacy of the Civil Rights Movement. After graduating from Francis Marion University in Florence, South Carolina, with his bachelor’s degree, he joined the NAACP as a field organizer for voter rights and empowerment while pursuing his Master’s of Divinity at the Interdenominational Theological Center. In his time with the NAACP, Williams traveled across the Black Belt, where he said he witnessed poverty and inequity up close. “Civil rights traditionally has been something that people have tried to separate from progressivism … but these movements are inseparable,” said Williams. “What I witnessed in the South as a worker in voter rights and voter empowerment and education, and as a regional representative for the NAACP, was that the conditions that created inequity still existed and needed to be confronted and challenged.” His work took him to Kenya, where he served as a program coordinator with the Presbyterian Church USA. In Nairobi, he supported the Green Belt Movement’s work against deforestation and its mission to highlight environmental justice as a tool for economic empowerment and self-determination. Now, as some Black and brown voters express concerns of being tokenized by traditional Democratic candidates, Williams plans to bring his experience working in racial justice circles to his new role. “I have worked in communities that have borne the brunt of failed promises from the current Democratic leadership,” Williams said. “I have opened the doors of my congregations to politicians and have experienced the absence of those politicians after the elections.” He continued: “Black communities have become destinations for environmental hazards and data centers. Unemployment has risen. Black federal employees have been targeted. The list goes on. I’ve pastored these people. I've prayed with them. I've listened to them as they've shed tears. Now I've decided I want to move from triage work to really transformational work.” Some of that work will require challenging other Black leaders. “Unfortunately, many of our Black politicians have become victims of corporate capture, and their voices have been taken by entities like AIPAC,” said Williams, referring to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. “They have not really been able to stand for the issues that are affecting the communities that that many of us are fighting for, and JD candidates are free from that, and they're free to take bold and significant action to move forward legislation.” But with the 2026 election cycle nearly over, the PAC is already brainstorming how to establish a strong progressive coalition for the 2028 presidential election. That will mean convincing the mainstream Democratic party that Justice Democrats have built a lasting coalition of the party’s base, said Williams. “We hope that the Democratic Party would see that we're developing a blueprint to show them how the base is being energized around the issues that are kitchen table issues that people want us to deal with,” said Williams. “It's not enough for us just to have a call to defeat a fascist president. We don't want a fascist president. We want him out, but we also want a vision of what America could look like when affordability, healthcare, civil rights, housing, and livable wages — all of those things are at the top of the political agenda,” he added. Williams succeeds current executive director and co-founder Alexandra Rojas, who will become president of Justice Democrats’ board and will support Williams as a senior adviser.
articles.headline: Justice Democrats announce new executive director

articles.body: Iowa Rep. Ashley Hinson took a swipe at the savings habits of millennials as she fielded a question Wednesday about Social Security during a Senate campaign debate. Hinson, the Republican candidate facing off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, was asked about ensuring the solvency of Social Security when she raised the broader prospect of savings by millennials, the demographic consisting of people born from 1981-1996. She said the country needed to have a “serious conversation” about “how young people are saving money,” as part of the discussion about the future of Social Security. “We also need to be talking about millennials saving money,” she later added. “Millennials are the worst group of savers in the country right now and have the least amount of savings. So those are ways where I think we can help have a bigger conversation around saving in general, planning for retirement and making sure we're all able to experience a robust retirement.” Hinson faces a tough race in Iowa against Turek amid a difficult political environment for Republicans. Voters are overwhelmingly pessimistic about the state of the economy and their own personal finances, and they support Social Security while being concerned about the program’s future . Hinson said she would not support cutting benefits and suggested creating a bipartisan commission to present suggestions to Congress to save the program. When pushed on her statement that “all options should be on the table,” she turned her attention to young people. “I think my dad and I had this discussion when I was in sixth grade, looking at a ledger book and trying to figure out, 'Hey, how are we going to make sure you're set up for your life?'” she said. “So we need to be having a conversation simultaneously to all solutions on the table, to make sure that it can stay solvent, while we're also talking about, 'How do we get more young people to save?'” "She has never and will never cut Social Security," Hinson campaign spokesperson Billy Fuerst said in a statement. Turek, when asked about Social Security, said he supports removing the payroll tax cap. “The best way we can keep this solvent is by taking off the cap,” Turek said. “Let's make sure that billionaires and large corporations are paying their fair share. That will move the needle in a very serious way to keep Social Security solvent.” Hinson disagreed. “The only thing I'm hearing from him is that the only solution to everything is to raise taxes,” she said.
articles.headline: Iowa’s Ashley Hinson slams the savings habits of millennials

articles.body: MO’ MONEY: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman has received dozens of contributions surpassing the legal limit in recent months. Blakeman has yet to refund roughly $360,000 to donors who have given to him above the cap, as POLITICO first reported on Monday . Gubernatorial candidates are allowed to raise $9,000 from individuals for each election — so $18,000 if they have both a primary and a general. Blakeman dodged a June election, so he’s required to give back any money he’s raised above $9,000. Many of the excess contributions came early in the election cycle. Knicks owner James Dolan, for example, gave $18,000 on Jan. 20, before it was known whether there would be a primary. But there have been at least 40 donations above the $9,000 limit that have come in since the Board of Elections certified the primary ballot on May 13, according to Blakeman’s disclosure reports. Many of those came well past the primary. An Eric Sternberg who used a Nassau County PO Box, for example, gave Blakeman $15,000 in the spring. A donor with the same name who used a nearby home address gave $18,000 on Aug. 19; three more $5,000 checks from those Eric Sternbergs were reported on Sept. 10. In addition to those 40 donations, there are several individuals who have gone over the limit by making multiple contributions. Former Republican Rep. Nan Hayworth, for example, gave $5,205.08 on May 22, then the same amount on July 31, bringing her total to $10,410.16 for the election cycle. The unusual figure appears to arise from another way the Blakeman campaign is going past the $9,000 cap. His donation page asks people to make a supplemental contribution to cover processing fees — so somebody giving $5,000 gets a request to give an additional $205.08. Attempting to donate $9,000 brings forth a suggested donation of $9,369.14. That exact amount has been given 22 times, including by Nassau resident — and one-time Trump administration official — Anthony Scaramucci. “Anyone who looks at campaign finance filings will see every campaign eating the cost for processing fees,” Democratic campaign finance lawyer Ben Kallos said. “I admire the creativity of trying to have donors eat those costs, but you can’t go over the limit.” POLITICO asked the Blakeman campaign about the refunds it owes on Monday. It replied on Tuesday without addressing the issue. “So many New Yorkers opened their wallets to support Bruce Blakeman that the state’s antiquated campaign finance system couldn’t keep up,” spokesperson Madison Spanodemos said. “The Board of Elections required the campaign to split its most recent finance report into multiple files since it included so much data, causing some contributions to appear multiple times.” The Public Campaign Finance Board said it’s not to blame. “Mr. Blakeman’s campaign is the only filer that experienced this issue,” Democratic co-director Brian Keegan said. “This is a user error, not a system error.” Spanodemos did not respond to questions about the large donations or what the committee’s actual war chest is. If every potential duplicate is removed from Blakeman's filing, his contribution total would fall by $292,000. That would lower his balance to a $114,000 deficit, even before accounting for the $360,000 in refunds he owes. A shift like that wouldn’t be unprecedented. Blakeman’s previous report, submitted on July 15, showed he had $4.7 million in the bank. An amended version submitted on July 22 changed his balance to $6.1 million. Yet another amendment on Aug. 13 said that his war chest in mid-July had actually been $4.3 million. Gov. Kathy Hochul has recently received a handful of contributions over the limit as well. But as has been the norm for gubernatorial candidates, her committee has returned surpluses: The New York State Council of Machinists, for example, gave $10,000 on Sept. 15 and got $1,000 back on Sept. 28. Hochul’s campaign has started to make Blakeman’s campaign finance foibles an issue in recent weeks. “It’s against the law,” state Democratic Committee Chair Jay Jacobs said of the Republican’s large contributions. “He’s desperate for money, and desperate people do desperate things. And I think to him, it’s more important he try to get elected than comply with the law.” — Bill Mahoney ONE WEEK AWAY: Mayor Zohran Mamdani ’s administration is pursuing a bold agenda to tame the city’s affordability crisis — making New York City a testing ground for progressives across the country. Join POLITICO’s New York Outlook: Affordability, Industry & The Economy in NYC on Oct. 14 for live conversations about the business and policy decisions being made today that will shape the city’s economic future. The lineup includes NYC Comptroller Mark Levine , New York City Economic Development Corp. CEO Anthony Shorris , New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin , Partnership for NYC CEO Steven Fulop , Citizens Budget Commission President Andrew Rein , Charles H. Revson Foundation President Maria Torres-Springer , and more. Register now to attend in person or watch the livestream . FROM CITY HALL MAMDANI’S OCT. 7 MESSAGE: Mamdani marked the third anniversary of Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023 attack by condemning the “horrific war crimes” that took place in Israel that day — and then proceeded to blast the American ally for the military campaign it launched in response. “On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he said in a written statement this morning. He then pivoted: “The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children … Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes.” Mamdani’s missive — which he also posted on X , where it had garnered nearly 11 million views as of early this afternoon — was consistent with how he has for years messaged regarding the events on and after Oct. 7. What’s remarkable is that he did it as mayor on a somber day — the kind of occasion for which elected officials typically deploy restraint. Today marked his first time commemorating the anniversary as mayor of New York City, home to the largest Jewish community outside Israel, swaths of which believe Mamdani has fomented antisemitism by accusing the country of commiting a genocide in Gaza, a charge Israeli leaders vehemently deny. Backlash to the mayor’s statement was swift. “It is like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists,” Danny Danon, Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, wrote on X in response to Mamdani’s comments. “We will not let this happen. We will remember those who were murdered, and we will never forget who was behind this massacre.” Rep. Dan Goldman, a fellow Democrat, called it a “reprehensible statement.” “In the guise of ‘grieving’ with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with,” Goldman wrote on X . “On this day of all days, the Mayor of the city with the largest Jewish population outside of Israel embraces extreme activism instead of balanced leadership.” A spokesperson for Mamdani declined to respond to such criticisms. The mayor is scheduled to attend an Oct. 7 remembrance vigil this evening. Hochul commemorated the anniversary by ordering the Israeli flag be hoisted on top of the Capitol in Albany. She also ordered that flags be flown at half mast at all state government buildings across New York. “It’s hard to fathom that it has been three years since the October 7 Hamas massacre. Three years since the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust,” the governor said in a statement. “The pain of that dark day has not faded. But neither has the strength, resilience and enduring hope of the Jewish people.” — Chris Sommerfeldt From the Capitol FEDERAL TAX CREDIT UNDER FIRE: New York’s legislative leaders are urging Hochul to reject a GOP-backed federal tax credit scholarship program, setting up a potential clash over the hot-button issue. The Treasury Department released a pair of rules for the initiative — which was included in President Trump’s sweeping 2025 tax-and-spending package — last week. The program would give donors to nonprofits that support educational expenses a dollar-for-dollar tax credit of up to $1,700 annually. Married taxpayers filing jointly could receive a credit of up to $3,400. In a statement Wednesday, state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins said the regulations would undercut the state’s ability to establish “meaningful guardrails,” leaving New York with little control over which schools and expenses qualify or how the funding is used. She also said it would allow the money to potentially flow to schools outside the state. “I am apprehensive about this federal proposal and have serious reservations about the potential impact it could have on public schools across New York State,” Stewart-Cousins said. “New York should not opt in to this program.” Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie also said Tuesday that his chamber will prioritize ensuring public schools are fully funded. “Public dollars should support public schools that serve all children and are accountable to the taxpayers who fund them,” Heastie said in a statement. “New York should opt out of the federal voucher program and continue investing in the public schools that educate the overwhelming majority of our children.” The city’s and state’s teachers unions, with which the Legislature is closely aligned, have also urged Hochul to reject the program . Spokespeople for the governor did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the opposition of legislative leaders. But Hochul has signaled support for the scholarship program. Ahead of the release of the regulations, her office said the credits could expand educational opportunities for public and private school students statewide “without diverting resources from public schools or state and local budgets.” The governor’s team also said public schools could benefit from the program. — Madina Touré FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL TAKING THE STAGE: A debate is on the books in the battleground race between Democratic Rep. Tom Suozzi and his Republican challenger, former Assemblymember Mike LiPetri. The debate, hosted by News 12, will air on Oct. 20. The station said that’s the only Long Island congressional debate it’s hosting after Democratic Rep. Laura Gillen and Chris Gallant, Republican Rep. Nick LaLota’s Democratic challenger, declined News 12’s invite for their respective races. Republican Rep. Andrew Garbarino’s campaign did not respond to its invite, the station said. Suozzi defeated LiPetri by 4 points in 2024. National Republicans are pouring millions into the seat in the final stretch of the race with the hope of flipping it this year. — Madison Fernandez POLL POSITION : Hochul leads Republican foe Bruce Blakeman by 11 points in a Marist University survey released this morning. Hochul, seeking a second full term, draws 53% in the poll; Blakeman stands at 42%. Voters by a 55% to 42% margin plan to support the Democratic congressional candidate, the survey found. The poll of 1,361 likely voters was conducted from Oct. 1 to Oct. 4. It has a 3.6 percentage point margin of error. — Nick Reisman IN OTHER NEWS — GROCERY BRANDING: Branding for Mamdani’s signature city-run grocery stores will be handled by the same Brooklyn design firm behind trendy products like Graza olive oil and Yellowbird hot sauce. ( New York Magazine ) — GENDER-AFFIRMING CARE: New York City plans to spend nearly $9 million on local organizations providing gender-affirming care to minors, after two major hospital systems in the city struck deals with the Trump administration to stop providing such care. ( Gothamist ) — MAKE POLITICS SEXY AGAIN: Long Island Democratic congressional candidate Chris Gallant is leaning into sexiness, after the New York Post revealed last month he had appeared in bondage photos more than a decade ago. ( The New York Times ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .
articles.headline: Blakeman’s campaign finance mess

articles.body: National Republicans have spent months trying to rescue Ken Paxton. He’s complicating that effort. Tensions are brewing with some Republicans after POLITICO published Paxton’s closed-door comments that “D.C.” Republicans were largely controlling his race . “He is welcome to raise his own money and say whatever he wants,” said one Republican involved in the Paxton rescue effort, who like others in this article was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “In fact, if he did that, he’d probably be winning right now and we wouldn’t need to spend all this money.” "This just seems like Paxton preparing to blame others for what might be one of the most embarrassing defeats in modern political history," said Carlos Curbelo, a former Florida GOP representative. Senate Republicans and top operatives didn’t want to be in this position in the first place. Many had warned that the Trump effort to unseat Sen. John Cornyn and back Paxton in the primary would cost Republicans hundreds of millions to drag Paxton across the finish line in the general election. Cornyn and Senate GOP groups spent millions of dollars on ads during the primary attacking Paxton over his series of scandals and warning he was a flawed candidate. Since then, the usual crowd of never-Paxton types has expanded into a wider circle of frustrated Republicans who are irked by the effort it’s taking to boost the scandal-plagued Senate candidate. And Paxton saying he doesn’t control his campaign messaging — alongside his remarks that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention hurt him politically — isn’t helping. Paxton also complained about the drag of the Iran war and high prices on his campaign in another closed-door recording that Axios published Wednesday . “Beggars can’t be choosers. He can try to raise federal money at a level that is necessary to save his candidacy at this point but his arms don’t reach that high,” said a Texas-based GOP consultant who’s closely monitoring multiple races. “As usual, he communicates something that is unhelpful, that is undisciplined, that is politically self-harmful and like most things, lacks any gratitude whatsoever.” The top Senate GOP super PAC, Trump’s aligned MAGA Inc. operation and other Republicans are pumping more than $200 million into the race to salvage Paxton’s campaign against Democrat James Talarico. Trump allies say they have worked hard to shore up Paxton, suggesting they’ve pushed donations toward the campaign and the larger GOP super PAC effort to avoid disaster in the Lone Star State. Trump plans to travel to Texas for the second time Wednesday to boost Paxton. Paxton allies have brushed off his latest closed-door comments, saying he was referring to GOP super PACs he’s not allowed to coordinate with as a candidate. The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment, though campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in response to POLITICO’s initial report of the audio that “AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority, which is why he’s on the ground every day.” But another Republican, a Trump ally working on the fundraising effort, said the national intervention isn’t overstepping. That person said the messaging guidance from the national GOP is standard for major Senate races and that Paxton “needs the help.” One national GOP operative involved in the Texas Senate race noted that the attorney general's lackluster fundraising early on left him vulnerable to Talarico’s attacks throughout the summer — especially over Paxton’s series of “self-inflicted” scandals, which have made him “toxic” with key voting blocs in the deep red state. “We warned them about this,” the GOP operative said. The Texas Senate race has sucked up oxygen, despite Trump winning the state in 2024 by double digits. And, the Senate map has kept expanding as Democrats have made gains in other typically red states, forcing Republicans to make critical decisions about where to allocate resources. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Republicans have said there are dedicated donors who are backing their effort to help Paxton, as they also try to shore up red seats across the map. Paxton, in the September meeting with donors, acknowledged Washington’s influence. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign … it’s all coming — you know — from D.C.,” Paxton told donors during a small fundraising event last month, according to the audio. Top GOP officials have tried to downplay Paxton’s comments. The White House referred POLITICO to the RNC when asked for comment. The RNC argued Paxton, in the audio, was referring to the super PACs he can’t coordinate with as a candidate. "This is fake news nonsense mixed with lazy reporting demonstrating a clear ignorance about how super PACs work. President Trump has called Ken Paxton the single greatest attorney general in history and has been clear he will do whatever it takes to make him the next senator from Texas,” RNC spokesperson Zach Kraft said in a statement. Trump, when speaking to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, said he hadn’t seen Paxton’s latest comments. He added that his midterm travel blitz has helped Paxton and other Republican candidates. “Ken’s doing much better now that I — everybody is — since starting three, four days ago, since starting the rallies. It’s brought a whole new awareness to how great the Republicans are doing, how great the economy is doing,” Trump said, touting investments and manufacturing. The president last week traveled to Texas and told the crowd that Paxton is a “pain in the ass sometimes” and later acknowledged he’s “a little controversial." But, he also warned the Texas crowd that Talarico would be “such a horror to your state,” adding, “we need the votes and I'm here for that, and I think we're going to win.” Vance also traveled to Texas, where he called Paxton an “amazing attorney general and your next senator.” Still, other Republicans have simply grown resigned to the state of the race, with Paxton needing all the aid he can get. “There is only so much we can do,” one senior Senate GOP aide said. “And I feel like we’re doing a lot.” The Paxton campaign told POLITICO it raised $18 million in the third quarter across the campaign and his joint fundraising committees. That’s roughly double his second-quarter total, though the campaign did not provide its cash-on-hand numbers, and Talarico has yet to release his fundraising haul. Paxton also announced a $20 million ad buy last week — a significant single media investment in the race. But he’s had to rely heavily on Trump, MAGA Inc. and the top Senate GOP super PAC to bail him out. Republicans have largely leaned on the Senate Leadership Fund, rather than the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC, to keep Paxton afloat. SLF is spending a Texas record-breaking $131 million sum through Oct. 12 and has pledged to continue to spend more through the final weeks of the election. MAGA Inc. is increasing some spending for Paxton and is expected to hit near $45 million by Oct. 12. If Paxton were to lose, Trump’s reaction and whether he chooses to distance himself from the rescue effort will be driven by media coverage, said a former Trump fundraiser. “If the media coverage related to election night and the autopsy a couple days afterwards is brutal towards Trump, like, horrible economy, inflation's not that much better than the last year of Joe Biden's ... he will lash out,” the person said. “But if the narrative is, it’s a midterm presidential, this is what normally happens … he'll move on as fast as he can and never talk about Ken Paxton again. It just depends what the coverage looks like post the November election.” Myah Ward contributed to this report.
articles.headline: Paxton’s latest audio leak is making things tough for national Republicans

articles.body: The 2026 House map continues to move further onto GOP terrain. But while Democrats are dreaming big, the GOP insists they can hold the majority. Score talked to the DCCC's Deputy Executive Director Will Van Nuys and the NRCC's Communications Director Will Kiley. The two operatives chose four under-the-radar races where they’re feeling good about their underdog candidates pulling off an upset. If these races flip, they know they’re having a good night. “We're not saying that this won't be a tough fight to the end, but we know we feel very good about where we stand,” Kiley said. “Our job is to make sure that we raise as much as we can to expand this battlefield as far as we can,” Van Nuys said. DEMOCRATS’ FOUR 'SLEEPER' SEATS CO-05 (Trump +9.1) Rep. Jeff Crank won this seat by 14 points in 2024 in his third bid for Congress. But Colorado Springs is “trending Democrats’ way” with fast growth of younger and Hispanic populations. That shift, along with Trump’s unpopularity, has Democrats hoping for a flip, Van Nuys says. IA-02 (Trump +10) Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson’s run for Senate has left this northeastern Iowa seat open for the taking, Van Nuys argues. Frustrations with beef imports, rising gas prices and the popularity of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand have Democrats hoping state Rep. Lindsay James can turn this seat blue. KY-06 (Trump +15) Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear is making it his personal mission to elect his former adviser and federal prosecutor Zach Dembo and flip Senate nominee Rep. Andy Barr’s Lexington-based seat. Dembo released an internal poll in late September showing him with a 5-point lead. WI-01 (Trump +4.5) Van Nuys says emergency room nurse Mitchell Berman is a “perfect contrast” in the blue-collar district to Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, an attorney and former plastics manufacturing executive. FOUR DISTRICTS WHERE THE GOP THINKS IT CAN SURPRISE NM-02 (Trump +1.8) Former Republican Rep. Yvette Herrell ran four cycles in a row. Now the GOP is betting on a fresh face: Greg Cunningham, a tattooed, motorcycle-driving Marine vet and ex-cop who’s running ads highlighting his Hispanic heritage in the Latino-heavy district. Republicans are spending big on the race. Kiley called Cunningham a “badass.” “Greg is a candidate who can continue to capture those voters and keep them coming our way,” he said. NY-03 (Trump +4.3) Republican former state Assemblymember Mike LiPetri came within 4 points of defeating Rep. Tom Suozzi (D-N.Y.) in 2024, and Republican Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman coasted to reelection last fall. Now Blakeman is running for governor, and Kiley says the statewide campaign can push LiPetri over the top in a rematch. The MAGA Inc.-affiliated No Going Back PAC has dropped a whopping $6 million into the district, with $2 million more from NRCC, though the CLF trimmed its own ad buy there Tuesday. “Last cycle, LiPetri came incredibly close with minimal to no outside investment,” Kiley said. “Now he has the investment and institutional support to get the job done.” AZ-01 (Trump +3.1) The DCCC’s preferred candidate lost to former Democratic state Rep. Amish Shah in the primary in this Phoenix and Scottsdale-area seat, and Kiley says that’s opened the door for the GOP to hold the seat. “The DCCC is lying if they said that Amish is the candidate they wanted,” Kiley said. Republicans nominated former Arizona Cardinals kicker and NFL commentator Jay Feely, and Kiley says Feely’s unique resume will boost him over the edge. Both parties are spending huge sums, with more than $31 million combined earmarked for the race. NV-03 (Trump +0.7) Republican Marty O’Donnell was the composer for the music in the popular video game Halo. He’s using that success to pour $3 million into his bid to flip this Las Vegas-area seat held by Democratic Rep. Susie Lee. The personal investments, along with outside GOP spending , eliminate a cash advantage past Democrats enjoyed in the district, Kiley said. “The resources are coming in to flip this seat because the GOP ecosystem can see how big of an opportunity it is,” he said. articles.body: <p>Un cara a cara entre Pedro Sánchez y Alberto Núñez Feijóo, un debate a cuatro con los candidatos de los principales partidos y otro con los portavoces de las fuerzas parlamentarias. El Partido Popular ha aceptado este viernes participar en esas tres citas televisivas, y ha abierto la puerta a una posible entrevista al líder conservador en Televisión Española, con motivo de las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre. En un comunicado, el PP <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-05/rtve-atresmedia-y-mediaset-ofrecen-un-debate-cara-a-cara-entre-sanchez-y-feijoo.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-05/rtve-atresmedia-y-mediaset-ofrecen-un-debate-cara-a-cara-entre-sanchez-y-feijoo.html">recoge la invitación de Mediaset para el cara a cara con Sánchez</a> y da la fecha del 16 de noviembre, primer lunes de la campaña electoral, para su celebración. Feijóo también tiene intención de acudir al debate de Atresmedia entre los candidatos de las cuatro formaciones con mayor representación parlamentaria y propone que se celebre el 26 de noviembre. La aceptación de este formato, que el presidente popular rechazó en los pasados comicios, supone un giro en la estrategia con respecto a la anterior campaña.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-09/feijoo-acepta-un-debate-cara-a-cara-con-sanchez-y-otro-a-cuatro-con-el-resto-de-candidatos.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, ha admitido este viernes que “ahora en España no se está garantizando el derecho a una vivienda digna” y ha reconocido que el Gobierno no tiene las “herramientas” para resolver la <a href="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-10-08/la-crisis-de-la-vivienda-preocupa-mucho-o-bastante-a-ocho-de-cada-diez-espanoles.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/economia/vivienda/2026-10-08/la-crisis-de-la-vivienda-preocupa-mucho-o-bastante-a-ocho-de-cada-diez-espanoles.html">crisis de la vivienda</a> que afronta el país. Es la razón, dice, por la que se han convocado elecciones. Puente ha asegurado en una entrevista en la <a href="https://cadenaser.com/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://cadenaser.com/">Cadena SER</a> que los sondeos que maneja el PSOE prevén que el 29 de noviembre los socialistas serán “la primera fuerza”, pese a que<a href="https://cadenaser.com/" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://cadenaser.com/"> las encuestas publicadas </a>en los últimos días sitúan al partido como el segundo más votado después del PP, que conseguiría 132 diputados.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-09/puente-reconoce-que-el-gobierno-no-tiene-las-herramientas-para-resolver-el-problema-de-la-vivienda-por-eso-se-han-convocado-elecciones.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Puente reconoce que el Gobierno “no tiene las herramientas” para resolver el problema de la vivienda: “Por eso se han convocado elecciones”

articles.body: <p>La petición del PP en precampaña electoral no ha surtido efecto. articles.body: <p>El espacio a la izquierda del PSOE parece empeñado en repetir la historia. A una semana de que expire el plazo para registrar las coaliciones a las generales del 29 de noviembre, el Frente Amplio se resiste a confirmar su candidato, no ha definido a los principales cabezas de lista y ni siquiera tiene claro qué partidos irán juntos más allá de Izquierda Unida, Más Madrid, Comuns y Movimiento Sumar. La exalcaldesa de Barcelona, Ada Colau, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-08/colau-dispuesta-a-liderar-frente-amplio-si-suma-a-mucha-mas-gente-como-podemos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-08/colau-dispuesta-a-liderar-frente-amplio-si-suma-a-mucha-mas-gente-como-podemos.html">recogió este jueves el guante</a> de la organización de la ministra Mónica García y se declaró dispuesta a liderar si hay un acuerdo con Podemos dentro, pero sin concretar tampoco por dónde. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-09/la-izquierda-vuelve-a-tropezar-con-la-piedra-de-la-unidad.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>En medio de la tensión en la izquierda por las <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-08/colau-dispuesta-a-liderar-frente-amplio-si-suma-a-mucha-mas-gente-como-podemos.html" target="_blank" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/catalunya/2026-10-08/colau-dispuesta-a-liderar-frente-amplio-si-suma-a-mucha-mas-gente-como-podemos.html">negociaciones para las generales</a>, Movimiento Sumar ha hecho este viernes un llamamiento a la calma. El partido que coordinan la portavoz parlamentaria del grupo, Verónica Barbero, y la secretaria de Estado de Derechos Sociales, Rosa Martínez, pide en un comunicado al resto de fuerzas del Frente Amplio —Más Madrid, Comuns e Izquierda Unida— “sentarse a dialogar y cooperar con discreción y generosidad”. La organización, además, anuncia que sus bases han elegido con un 98% de los apoyos a Barbero para que sea el referente del partido en las listas del 29 de noviembre. La nueva coalición aún no ha oficializado a su líder ni cerrado los acuerdos con otras organizaciones del grupo parlamentario como Més y Chunta Aragonesista. Compromís ya ha anunciado su intención de presentarse con una coalición propia valenciana. Y tampoco ha <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-08/la-propuesta-para-que-colau-lidere-el-frente-amplio-en-las-generales-reabre-el-debate-sobre-el-encaje-de-podemos.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-08/la-propuesta-para-que-colau-lidere-el-frente-amplio-en-las-generales-reabre-el-debate-sobre-el-encaje-de-podemos.html">resuelto el encaje de Podemos</a>, cuya presencia ha exigido como condición la exalcaldesa de Barcelona, Ada Colau, para liderar el espacio.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-09/movimiento-sumar-llama-al-resto-de-partidos-del-frente-amplio-a-negociar-con-discrecion-y-generosidad.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
articles.headline: Movimiento Sumar llama al resto de partidos del Frente Amplio a negociar con “discreción y generosidad”

articles.body: <p>Las casitas del humilde barrio de El Príncipe están pintadas con colores intensos. Hay verdes, grises, rosas, azuladas... Todas forman un entramado de callejuelas estrechas que confluyen en varias plazas y de las que sobresalen los minaretes de las mezquitas. Ahora, en sus rincones se resguardan decenas de migrantes que llegaron con la entrada masiva a Ceuta y que no quieren retornar a Marruecos. Algunos llevan solo unos días asentados en el vecindario: son migrantes que vienen de El Trampolín huyendo de la Policía <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-06/el-desalojo-de-la-playa-de-el-trampolin-dispara-los-regresos-voluntarios-en-ceuta-900-retornos-en-un-dia.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-06/el-desalojo-de-la-playa-de-el-trampolin-dispara-los-regresos-voluntarios-en-ceuta-900-retornos-en-un-dia.html">tras el reciente desalojo del asentamiento instalado en la playa</a>. Otros dormitan en las calles o se cobijan en sus casitas de colores ya desde el inicio de la crisis. Entre quienes se han internado en El Príncipe se encuentra Tamo, una mujer marroquí de 35 años, y sus cinco hijas pequeñas. Todas entraron juntas a nado a la ciudad autónoma a finales de julio. Hoy buscan refugio.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-09/el-barrio-de-el-principe-refugio-de-los-migrantes-que-no-quieren-abandonar-ceuta.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/NUUZMFGRS5FO3GKC5XJU2EYSO4.jpg?auth=5f50138ed94d32a300a080a491221e9fab906f218c37d3b9eabff748baac6f82" width="3648" height="2432" alt="Tamo y sus hijas, en El Príncipe."></img><img src="https://imagenes.elpais.com/resizer/v2/IQEVTJFCSZDP3MNN3YQO2ZVRIY.jpg?auth=ebb961df43c084a90c8d44e9e3a008785e458fb37ba0b54da7f4f3b12e3c4a9e" width="3648" height="2432" alt="Ahmed Enfed-Dal con menores, en El Príncipe."></img>
articles.headline: Tamo y sus cinco hijas, a la búsqueda de refugio en el barrio de El Príncipe tras llegar a nado a Ceuta

articles.body: <p>Adriana Lastra regresa a la primera línea de la política española. La ex vicesecretaria general del PSOE y exportavoz en el Congreso será la número uno de su partido en las listas al Congreso por Asturias en las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre. La ejecutiva autonómica que lidera el presidente del Principado, Adrián Barbón, ha tomado por unanimidad la decisión, que cuenta además con el beneplácito de Ferraz. “Es la mejor candidata”, ha valorado la Federación Socialista Asturiana (FSA), con muchos menos militantes que otros territorios pero un enorme peso orgánico e institucional por ser uno de los baluartes del PSOE en los buenos y malos momentos. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-08/adriana-lastra-encabezara-lista-del-psoe-al-congreso-por-asturias-el-29-n.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Poco después de que saltase la noticia de que Maricarmen Abascal <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-07/muere-maricarmen-la-mujer-que-encendio-la-lucha-contra-los-desahucios-en-espana.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-07/muere-maricarmen-la-mujer-que-encendio-la-lucha-contra-los-desahucios-en-espana.html">había fallecido</a>, una de sus vecinas del edificio de Sainz de Baranda rebuscó en un cajón un pedazo de papel adhesivo para escribir unas líneas. Luego, se acercó a la puerta de la casa donde la mujer de 87 años había vivido las últimas siete décadas antes de ser desahuciada y lo pegó. “Descansa en paz, Maricarmen”, decía el pequeño cartel. Debajo de esa frase también había dibujado un corazón con rotulador negro. Sacó una foto para enviarla a unos familiares y regresó entre lágrimas a su casa. “Maricarmen ha perdido la vida luchando”, cuenta esta vecina, que pide no ser identificada.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/madrid/2026-10-08/los-vecinos-recuerdan-a-maricarmen-era-una-persona-muy-vital-el-desahucio-acabo-con-ella.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>El Gobierno español ha decidido posponer la reunión de alto nivel con Argelia, cuya celebración estaba prevista este mes en Madrid. Aunque no se había fijado una fecha definitiva, su reanudación <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-20/espana-y-argelia-acuerdan-celebrar-en-octubre-su-primera-reunion-de-alto-nivel-desde-hace-ocho-anos.html" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-07-20/espana-y-argelia-acuerdan-celebrar-en-octubre-su-primera-reunion-de-alto-nivel-desde-hace-ocho-anos.html">fue pactada para octubre </a>por el presidente argelino,<a href="https://elpais.com/noticias/abdelmajid-tebun/" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/noticias/abdelmajid-tebun/"> Abdelmayid Tebún,</a> y el jefe del Gobierno español, Pedro Sánchez, durante la visita de este último a Argel en julio, apenas 10 días antes de que estallara la crisis en Ceuta. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-08/el-gobierno-pospone-la-reunion-de-alto-nivel-con-argelia-en-visperas-de-la-visita-del-rey-a-ceuta-y-melilla.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: <p>Ecuador ha detenido en un gran operativo policial a los responsables del envío de un contenedor de 13 toneladas de cocaína que llevó hasta el supuesto capo Ignacio Torán y al jefe policial de Madrid detenido con <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-06-13/el-album-inedito-de-los-zulos-del-anodino-el-policia-que-escondia-millones-de-euros-del-narco-entre-sus-paredes.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-06-13/el-album-inedito-de-los-zulos-del-anodino-el-policia-que-escondia-millones-de-euros-del-narco-entre-sus-paredes.html">millones de euros emparedados en su casa</a>. Este cargamento, interceptado en Algeciras (Cádiz), se convirtió <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2025-04-03/contenedor-tclu1210545-el-rastro-que-dejo-el-mayor-alijo-de-cocaina-de-la-historia-de-espana.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2025-04-03/contenedor-tclu1210545-el-rastro-que-dejo-el-mayor-alijo-de-cocaina-de-la-historia-de-espana.html">en el mayor alijo de la historia de España hasta octubre de 2024</a>, luego superado <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-05-03/la-guardia-civil-intercepta-en-alta-mar-un-carguero-con-un-gigantesco-alijo-de-cocaina.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-05-03/la-guardia-civil-intercepta-en-alta-mar-un-carguero-con-un-gigantesco-alijo-de-cocaina.html">por las 30 toneladas interceptadas</a> en alta mar por la Guardia Civil el pasado mayo. </p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/2026-10-08/detenidos-en-ecuador-los-traficantes-del-gran-alijo-de-cocaina-que-precipito-el-caso-del-narcopolicia-con-millones-de-euros-emparedados.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>

articles.body: Arriba la festa de la Castanyada 2026 i el Halloween a Barcelona ! Els diferents barris de la ciutat han preparat desenes d’activitats per viure la nit més terrorífica de l’any, celebrar la Castanyada i la nit de Tots Sants. Prepara la teva disfressa de por, els panellets i les castanyes i suma’t a la proposta que més t’agradi! Et detallem què fer a Barcelona per la Castanyada i Halloween 2026. Halloween 2026 al Poble Espanyol Creepy Family El Poble Espanyol et proposa gaudir del Halloween ! Torna Creepy per celebrar el Halloween 2026 , que atemorirà un any més els visitants. L’espectacle ofereix la versió diürna, dirigida al públic familiar (versió Haunted ) i una altra a partir de la tarda vespre, més apropiada per a un públic jove i adult (versió Scream ). Quan?: 17, 18, 24 i 25 i 31 d’octubre i 1 de novembre, de 10 a 17 h i de 17 a 21 h. Preu: de 12,5 a 16,5 €. Què has de saber?: segons l’horari que escullis per entrar als túnels misteriosos, el nivell de por variarà: – de 10 h a 18 h versió HAUNTED, amb un enfocament més lúdic i un nivell d’ensurts suau (recomanat a partir de 3 anys). -de 18 h a 21 h versió SCREAM, amb una mica més d’intensitat, per a qui busca emocions més fortes (recomanat a partir de 7 anys). La Zona El Poble Espanyol obre les portes de La Zona, la seva experiència de terror més pertorbadora. Quan?: 16 i 23 d’octubre (a les 20 h), 30 d’octubre (a les 19 h) i 31 d’octubre (a les 20.30 h). Última entrada de 23 a 23.40 h, depèn de l’aforament. Preu: a partir de 24 €. Què has de saber?: és aconsellable ser major d’edat, si ets menor, has d’entrar acompanyat per un adult Festa Mascarada El Poble Espanyol organitza també la quarta edició de la  festa Mascarada. Una nit amb una  acurada selecció musical i en la qual s’anima els assistents a  portar una màscara  per submergir-se en el concepte de Mascarada. Dissabte 31 d’octubre, a la nit. Halloween 2026 al Tibidabo El Tibidabo es vesteix de Halloween !, aquí algunes de les propostes: L’Últim Ball:  és un  espectacle de por per a totes les edats on els zombis més terrorífics envaeixen el Tibidabo. Del 3 d’octubre al 8 de novembre . Inclòs amb entrada al parc. Dissabtes a les 20.30 h i diumenges a les 19.30 h. Hotel 666 : L’hotel més misteriós de Barcelona et dona la benvinguda perquè visquis una estada única. Passeja per les habitacions d’un hotel abandonat en el qual habiten  personatges icònics del cinema del terror . Diferents horaris dies d’obertura del parc. Beyond : l’ atracció de realitat virtual immersiva , també s’apunta a la temporada de Halloween. Descobreix  Traumatika , una experiència de terror única i plena de zombis. Túnel del terror a la Trinitat Vella 2026 Ja és tot un clàssic! Torna el túnel més terrorífic ! El trobaràs a la Trinitat Vella, en concret al Centre Cívic. Quan? La cita serà el divendres 30 d’octubre de 2026 , de 19 a 0 h. A partir dels 8 anys. Amb reserva prèvia presencial al Centre Cívic de Trinitat Vella fins al 9 d’octubre. Entrades prioritàries pels veïns de Trinitat Vella. “HalloQueer” 2026 L’Esquerra de l’Eixample celebrarà una nova edició del Halloween de la diversitat, la igualtat i la unió. El Gaixample acollirà una fira amb els comerços de barri, entitats i artesans. Quan? Dissabte 24 d’octubre de 2026, a la plaça d’Universitat Horari : D’11 a 1 h Què has de saber?: Hi haurà de tot vermutada, concerts, bingo, maquillatge de terror, drag queen i molt més Castanyera a La Pedrera Aquesta any la Castanyera visita La Pedrera i omple l’edifici d’objectes de la tardor! Sabràs trobar-los a dins de la casa més singular d’Antoni Gaudí? Descobreix La Pedrera a través de reptes. Activitat els dies 10, 12, 17, 24 i 31 d’octubre, a les 10 h . Entrades, 9.50 € (menors de 3 anys, gratuït). Concert de Halloween al Palau de la Música: Psicosi El Palau de la Música programa una nova edició del concert de Tots Sants amb Cinema de terror, a càrrec de l’Orquestra Simfònica del Vallès. Dissabte, 31 d’octubre, a les 18.30 h . Sessió sorpresa per halloween, al Phenomena La sala de cinema Phenomena torna a programar una sessió doble sorpresa , per la nit de halloween. Projectaran dues pel·lícules de terror, a partir de les 22 h. Halloween als Encants i Túnel del Terror Un any més el Mercat dels Encants celebra Halloween! El 30 y 31 de octubre no t’ho pensis i entra a Circus, un passatge terrorífic ambientat en la història dels Encants. Un antic circ ha despertat i els seus personatges estan esperant que hi vagis… t’hi atreveixes? I aconseguiràs sortir…? Estigues al cas al web del Mercat dels Encants, perquè hi trobaràs molt aviat les reserves disponibles ! >> Divendres 30, de 16 a 19 h i dissabte 31, d’11 a 14 i 16 a 19 h. Nit d’Ànimes de Porta Saps que a Porta preparen cada any, a Can Verdaguer, activitats per a tots els gustos i edats per celebrar la castanyada i halloween? Divendres 23 i dissabte, 24 d’octubre (gratuït), Plaça de Sóller. Divendres 23 d’octubre, castanyada infantil. 17.30 h: tallers de manualitats, beguda terrorífica, queimada i castanyada. | 18.30 h: túnel de terror infantil, per a menors de 14 anys i apte per a persones amb alta sensibilitat a llum i colors. Dissabte 24 d’octubre, túnel de la por. 18 h: Contenció 13 (per a majors de 14 anys). Una experiència de terror per a persones adultes que posarà a prova la vostra capacitat per sortir-ne, els sistemes de contenció fallen i les cel·les s’han obert… L’últim grup podrà entrar a les 20.30 h. Espectacle familiar al Magatzem d’Ars Una castanyada de por és l’espectacle familiar del Magatzem d’Ars per aquests dies de Tots Sants. Els més petits podran gaudir d’una història que gira al voltant de la història de la castanyera , que, com cada any, baixa de la muntanya i quan arriba a la ciutat s’adona que els nens estan més interessats en les disfresses i les llaminadures de Halloween. Per evitar que l’oblidin, la castanyera pren una sèrie de decisions, algunes poc encertades. Dissabtes i diumenges, del 17 d’octubre a l’1 de novembre. Gran Social Halloween al Casino l’Aliança No et perdis el programa d’activitats que han preparat al Casino l’Aliança del Poblenou, amb concurs de disfresses inclòs! Una festa diferent de halloween, on ballar salsa, timba cubana, bachata i música de DJ Papi. Una festa per ballar de por! 22.30 h: Taller Misteriós de Ball 23 h: Salsa & Bachata Session amb Animacions a càrrec de La Casa Del Son 1.30 h: Concurs de Disfresses 2 h: Closing Retro Hits & Latin Commercial Embruixat Cursa de bèsties de foc dels diables del Clot Coincidint amb aquestes dates els diables del Clot celebren la seva cursa de bèsties de foc (dins la festa major). Si no ets de castanyes ni halloween… aprofita aquesta cita que coincideix per dates! 31 d’octubre, a les 17 h, al carrer de Consell de Cent (Entre Independència i Meridiana). Escape room terrorífics Els coneguts popularment com a escape room continuen tenint molts seguidors. N’hi ha per a tots els gustos: de ciència, fantasia, intriga i, evidentment, també n’hi ha de por. Mira, remena i tria el que més t’agradi… o el que més por et faci! Festes als carrers de Gràcia i Sants Les comissions dels carrers que guarneixen per la Festa Major de Gràcia i per la Festa Major de Sants , també organitzen les seves pròpies festes (podeu trobar tota la informació a les seves xarxes socials): Carrer Verdi del Mig (Gràcia): Dissabte 31 d’octubre. Festa de la castanyada i dia de morts. 12 h vermut musical. 17 h castanyada i muntatge de l’altar. 18 h tardeo. 20 h botifarrada i DJ a les 22 h. Ves-hi disfressat i porta el teu got! Carrer de la Perla (Gràcia): Dissabte 31 d’octubre. Dia de Morts. 19 h. Tacos, música i altar de morts. Carrer Llibertat (Gràcia): Dissabte 31 d’octubre. Castaween. 18 h. Ets més de castanyada o de halloween? no escullis! Consulta més festes de la Castanyada als centres cívics de la ciutat Castanyada als barris (pendent d’actualitzar) Els diferents barris de la ciutat es bolquen per celebrar la castanyada, amb infinitat de propostes gratuïtes. Aquí pots consultar els enllaços del recull d’activitats que es fan, per districtes . La comunitat establerta a Barcelona ho celebra per difondre la cultura del Dia de Morts de Mèxic. Les “Catrinas” fan una passejada per la Rambla i un jurat valora i entrega premis el maquillatge, el vestuari, l’originalitat, l’ús d’elements reciclats, i entregarà premis a les figures més originals. Altar del Dia dels Morts, al Consolat de Mèxic de Barcelona (pendent d’actualitzar) A Mèxic, el dia de Tots Sants  se celebra de manera molt diferent . Se l’anomena el  Dia de Morts  i és una jornada festiva per recordar els difunts. Els mexicans instal·len  altars en honor dels morts de la família , on s’ofrenen aliments, espelmes, flors i objectes d’ús quotidià del difunt. Per això, un any més, el Consolat de Mèxic a Barcelona torna a fer l’Altar del Dia de Morts, obert a visites. Nit d’Ànimes, al Museu Marítim (pendent d’actualitzar) La Nit de les Ànimes a l’MMB és un clàssic per aquestes dates! Esperits infames que perpetuen injustícies, objectes insòlits que apareixen del no-res, ombres que es desplacen pel Museu en arribar la nit, sorolls inquietants… Un joc de proves terrorífiques al Museu per participar en equips. Activitat gratuïta amb aforament limitat. Divendres, 24 d’octubre de 2025, en dos torns, de 21 a 22.30 h i de 23 a 0.30 h . Durada:  1.30 h per torn. Edat:  a partir de 14 anys (Els menors d’edat han de venir acompanyats per un adult). Gratuït amb reserva. Passatge Terrorífic i Ruta Truc o Tracte de SOM Sant Antoni (pendent d’actualitzar) Dijous 30 d’octubre 2025: Un any més, entra al passatge terrorífic dels comerços del barri de Sant Antoni i passa-hi molta por! Atents perquè canvia d’ubicació! L’ entrada és gratuïta per als infants de fins a 120 cm i també podràs aconseguir passis gratuïts comprant a les botigues de SOM Sant Antoni, Encants o Mercat de Sant Antoni. A més hi haurà photocall i concurs de disfresses amb 3 premis! Dijous, 30 d’octubre, de 17 a 21 h, a la plaça de Conxa Pérez (davant el Mercat). Per saber quins hi participen, podràs consultar el full de mà que es repartirà al passatge del terror (i que si segelles als establiments entraràs en un sorteig amb premi final), o també a les xarxes socials. Festa de la castanyada als Jardins de Can Farrero (pendent d’actualitzar) Castanyes, festa i molt de ritme faran d’aquesta festa popular i tradicional la més divertida de La Marina. Hi haurà un munt d’activitats, entre les quals una animació musical per a tota la família (ZUM del grup d’animació La Tresca i La Verdesca), i castanyes calentes per a tothom. També celebrem la Setmana Mundial de l’Espai i descobrim per què els astronautes floten a l’espai i aprenem què vol dir orbitar la Terra. A més, el Mag Stigman ens sorprèn amb un joc de multiplicació de monedes, el Jordi Montserrat ens porta el ‘ MeteoKrac ‘ i al ‘ Paraules a la vista ‘ descobrim què significa la paraula “potiner”.
